analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical makers to prove their products are safe before selling them.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 41 House sponsors and cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing, but never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Toxic Chemicals Safety Act of 2010 would have rewritten the nation's main chemical safety law for the first time since 1976. It would have required chemical manufacturers to submit health and safety data for their products and to bear the burden of proving each chemical is safe, starting with a priority list of at least 300 chemicals that includes bisphenol A (BPA), formaldehyde, hexavalent chromium, and plastic-softening phthalates. It would have banned several flame retardants known to persist in the environment, created a public database of chemical toxicity and exposure, and given special attention to children, pregnant women, and workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, children, and workers. Anyone exposed to chemicals whose safety has never been fully reviewed would gain, because manufacturers would have to show a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' before a chemical could stay on the market, with specific protection for vulnerable groups. Workers would gain from explicit occupational exposure controls, and communities near manufacturing would gain from a program identifying localities with disproportionate exposure.

how_it_helps.text: Shifts the burden of proof onto chemical manufacturers and processors, who must demonstrate a chemical meets a safety standard of 'reasonable certainty that no harm will result' for all intended uses, rather than requiring the EPA to prove harm first.

Requires safety determinations for a priority list of at least 300 chemicals, starting immediately with 13 named substances including BPA, formaldehyde, hexavalent chromium, trichloroethylene, vinyl chloride, and seven phthalates.

Bans the manufacture, processing, use, and disposal of several persistent toxic substances, including hexachlorobenzene, hexabromobiphenyl, and two commercial flame retardant mixtures (PentaBDE and OctaBDE components).

Requires manufacturers to file declarations identifying exposed workers and facilities, disclose health and safety studies, and give commercial purchasers the chemical identity and toxicological information for what they buy.

Creates a searchable public database of chemical toxicity, use, and exposure information, and requires biomonitoring of pregnant women and infants for chemicals likely to affect early childhood development.
Directs the EPA to identify localities disproportionately exposed to toxic chemicals and develop action plans to reduce that exposure, and to fund research on children's vulnerability to chemicals.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and processors, who would bear the cost of generating minimum data sets and testing for thousands of chemicals, proving safety within deadlines (18 months for the initial 13 chemicals), and losing sales for chemicals that fail. Some costs would likely be passed to downstream manufacturers and consumers through higher prices, and useful products containing restricted chemicals could disappear or be reformulated.

drawbacks.text: The testing and data-generation burden is large: manufacturers would have had to compile minimum data sets for high-, moderate-, and low-volume chemicals on staggered 3-to-5-year deadlines and prove safety for a constantly maintained list of at least 300 priority chemicals, costs that would fall partly on downstream product makers and consumers as higher prices.

The bill allows 'critical use' exemptions where a restriction would significantly disrupt the national economy or no safer alternative exists, which could keep restricted chemicals in circulation for renewably 5-year periods, and it lets the EPA exempt substances scientific consensus deems harmless — giving a regulator considerable discretion in both directions.

The EPA would need substantially more resources and scientific capacity to process hundreds of safety determinations on statutory deadlines; the bill's own remedy for missed deadlines is to prohibit new uses of the chemical, which could freeze markets if the agency falls behind.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the potential gain is large: Americans carry chemicals in their bodies whose safety has never been adequately reviewed, and this bill would have reversed the default so industry had to show safety. The cost is real but ordinary — testing, reformulation, and compliance spending by manufacturers, some passed to consumers — and the bill built in exemptions for critical uses. The bill's design was more aggressive than the reform Congress eventually enacted in 2016, which kept the burden of proof largely on the EPA.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee, which held one hearing on July 29, 2010, but no markup or floor vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on July 22, 2010, joined by Reps. Waxman, Castor, DeGette, Schakowsky, and Sarbanes as original introducers.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on July 26, 2010 to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, which held a hearing on July 29, 2010.
Forty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and no further action was recorded after the July 29, 2010 subcommittee hearing; it expired with the 111th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they avoided a requirement to prove the safety of chemicals they had sold for decades without full testing, and avoided bans on specific flame retardants and priority chemicals. Consumers and workers remain under the 1976 law, which put the burden on the EPA to prove harm.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers that avoided new testing duties

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced to a vote where party splits would be recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required manufacturers to generate safety data and prove each chemical harmless before sale, with bans on specific persistent toxic substances — reversing the 1976 default under which the EPA must prove harm. It died, so the industry kept the existing structure.

industries.industry: Downstream product makers (manufacturers using chemicals in goods)
industries.note: They would have faced new disclosure duties to commercial purchasers and possible reformulation costs, but also gained reliable public information about the chemicals they buy and certainty that inputs meet a safety standard.
The bill would have created incentives and exemptions for approved safer alternatives, expanding the market for substitutes that reduce hazardous chemical use.
